 Chemical Sunscreen Lobby Accused of Impersonating Charity to Discredit Sunscreen Chemical Safety Concerns
 Issued by Australian Sunscreen Council 
 Media contact ↓ 
 ACCC complaint alleges industry lobby group Accord Australasia sought to discredit the legitimacy of the Australian Sunscreen Council, a charity that published research showing that two chemicals used by some of its members were unsafe. The lobby group publicly describes itself as “independent of any individual product, ingredient, or commercial interest”, while promising paying members it will advocate for their interests and help them gain influence over government policy.
 BRISBANE, 19 November 2026 — The Australian Sunscreen Council has lodged a complaint with the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) REF4796464, alleging that chemical sunscreen industry lobby group Accord Australasia engaged in misleading conduct by registering the charity’s name as its own business name, claiming to be the organisation and attempting to discredit its concerns about chemical sunscreen safety.
Accord Australasia describes itself publicly as:
“Independent of any individual product, ingredient, or commercial interest.”
Yet its own membership material tells prospective members:
“We champion our members by advocating for their interests.”
It also promises members they will:
“Gain influence and insight on policies shaping your operating environment.”
Accord Australasia’s board includes senior executives from L’Oréal, Procter & Gamble, Kao, Beiersdorf, Unilever, Estée Lauder, Coty, LVMH and Colgate-Palmolive, among others. These corporate groups own or market major sunscreen brands including La Roche-Posay, Olay, Bioré, Bondi Sands and NIVEA Sun.
The Australian Sunscreen Council alleges that Accord Australasia registered “Australian Sunscreen Council” as a business name in an attempt to pretend to be the charity and discredit its name to the public and journalists. In Australia, a business name registration is separate to a trademark and does not give you copyright.
Accord’s Executive Director, lobbyist Damian Mitsch, published a statement declaring: “We are the Australian Sunscreen Council.” Mr Mitsch also publicly questioned the charity’s legitimacy, reportedly writing on LinkedIn: “It appears to be a fake association.”
The charity alleges that the registration and subsequent statements formed part of an attempt to undermine its credibility and confuse journalists, regulators and the public about the identity of the organisation raising legitimate chemical sunscreen safety concerns.
 Chemical Industry Lobbying: A Familiar Pattern?
“People have seen this before with the tobacco industry and PFAS manufacturers. When scientific concerns emerge about profitable chemicals, industry lobbyists challenge the concerns and the people raising them,” said Joseph Mizikovsky, a director and major supporter of the Australian Sunscreen Council and CEO of Australian sunscreen manufacturer VeganicSKN.
“Accord is about as independent a voice on chemical sunscreen safety as the Tobacco Institute was on cigarettes.”
 Lobbyist Compares Hormone-Disrupting Sunscreen Chemical to Beer at Kindergartens
When challenged over concerns about the use of the hormone-disrupting sunscreen chemical 4-MBC in kindergartens, Accord Australasia Executive Director Damian Mitsch reportedly sought to downplay those concerns by comparing the chemical’s hormonal effects with those of beer, writing:
“Yet we don’t see signs trying to scare people off the hoppy brew at … kindergartens.”
The comparison stands in stark contrast to the findings of European scientific authorities, which have identified significant concerns about 4-MBC’s effects on the endocrine system.
In its 2022 safety assessment, the European Commission’s Scientific Committee on Consumer Safety (SCCS) concluded there was sufficient evidence that 4-MBC may act as an endocrine disruptor, affecting both the thyroid and oestrogen systems. The committee was unable to establish a safe maximum concentration because the available evidence could not exclude potential genetic damage.
4-MBC: What the Scientific Evidence Shows
Hormone disruption: Scientific assessments have identified endocrine-disrupting properties involving the thyroid and oestrogen systems.
Thyroid effects: Animal studies have reported thyroid enlargement and changes in thyroid function, including following prenatal exposure.
Oestrogenic activity: Laboratory studies have demonstrated oestrogen-like effects, including increased uterine weight in animals and proliferation of certain human breast cancer cells.
Developmental effects: Animal studies have reported changes in sexual development, reproductive organs, behaviour and hormone-receptor expression following prenatal exposure.
Human exposure: 4-MBC or its metabolites have been detected in human biological samples, including urine and breast milk.
Unresolved genetic safety: European regulators could not exclude genotoxic potential and therefore could not establish a safe maximum concentration for its use as a cosmetic UV filter.
International restrictions: The Australian Sunscreen Council has documented restrictions, prohibitions or non-approval of 4-MBC across 109 jurisdictions, including major sunscreen markets.
Australia’s Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) is currently considering regulatory options for 4-MBC, including a complete prohibition on its use in therapeutic goods and cosmetics.
“While European scientists have identified serious concerns about this chemical’s effects on the hormonal system, we have an Australian chemical industry lobbyist comparing concerns about its use in kindergartens to beer,” Mr Mizikovsky said.
“Parents deserve scientific evidence that the sunscreen chemicals being applied to their children are safe. They should not have their legitimate concerns dismissed with jokes about beer at kindergartens.”
ACCC Asked to Investigate
The Australian Sunscreen Council has asked the ACCC to investigate the conduct of Accord Australasia and its Executive Director Damian Mitsch, including:
Accord’s registration and use of the Australian Sunscreen Council name.
Alleged representations that Accord was the Australian Sunscreen Council, or that the charity itself was not legitimate.
Public claims of independence despite Accord’s stated role in advocating for its members’ commercial interests.
Representations concerning the safety of chemical sunscreen ingredients and their environmental impacts, including coral reefs.
The Australian Sunscreen Council is operated by Australian Sun Protection Institute Ltd, an ACNC-registered charity dedicated to independent research, public education and evidence-based information about sunscreen safety, ultraviolet radiation and the health effects of UV exposure.
Unlike a sunscreen industry lobby group, the charity’s purpose is not to promote sunscreen consumption or protect commercial interests. Its work includes examining both the benefits and risks of UV exposure, including circumstances where the scientific evidence may support reduced sunscreen use in the interests of public health.
The complaint concerns Accord Australasia and Mr Mitsch. The charity makes no allegation of wrongdoing against Accord’s individual directors or their companies.
The allegations have been referred to the ACCC. The ACCC has not made any findings of wrongdoing.

 About the Australian Sunscreen Council
The Australian Sunscreen Council is a registered Australian charity dedicated to improving the health of everyday Australians through UV education, research and evidence-based sun safety initiatives.
As Australia’s peak industry body for sunscreen safety, the Council works with scientists, medical professionals, industry experts and policymakers to advance sunscreen safety, support independent research, improve public understanding of UV exposure and promote stronger public-health standards.
